items.stem: A pond with its fish, plants, insects, water and mud is an example of a(n)…
items.answer: ecosystem
items.markingKey: D. Living plus non-living.

items.stem: Distinguish between an ecosystem and a habitat.
items.answer: A habitat is where an organism lives; an ecosystem is the whole system of living organisms and their non-living surroundings interacting.
items.markingKey: A habitat is where an organism lives; an ecosystem is the whole system of living organisms and their non-living surroundings interacting. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Abiotic factors are not important because they are not alive." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Abiotic factors such as temperature, water and light control which organisms can survive in a habitat.
items.markingKey: Abiotic factors such as temperature, water and light control which organisms can survive in a habitat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Yusuf counted the number of woodlice under logs at different distances from a stream (three logs at each distance).

Distance from stream / m | Woodlice per log: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 37 | 38 | 37
3 | 28 | 29 | 29
5 | 20 | 21 | 20
7 | 13 | 13 | 13
9 | 4 | 4 | 4

State the distance from stream at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 1 m; range = 1; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 1 m; 1 range = max − min = 38 − 37 = 1; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Maya is investigating how light intensity affects the number of daisy plants in different parts of a school field. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: light intensity at ground level (lux, measured with a light meter)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: light intensity at ground level (lux, measured with a light meter) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Building a new road through a forest should be allowed if a wildlife bridge is built."
items.answer: Wildlife bridges reduce harm but do not remove it; alternatives that avoid the forest should be considered first.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: bridges allow animals to cross safely; roads bring economic benefits. Arguments against: habitat is still lost and fragmented; noise, pollution and road kill continue; not all species use bridges. Supported judgement: Wildlife bridges reduce harm but do not remove it; alternatives that avoid the forest should be considered first.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "population"?
options: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time
Choosing sample positions by chance (e.g. random coordinates) to avoid bias
The percentage of a quadrat’s area covered by a particular species
items.answer: All the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time
items.markingKey: B. "population" is all the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time.

items.stem: Explain why the population of a species in a habitat cannot keep increasing forever.
items.answer: Resources such as food, water and space are limited; as numbers rise, competition, predation and disease increase until births and deaths balance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Resources such as food, water and space are limited; as numbers rise, competition, predation and disease increase until births and deaths balance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Wolves return to Yellowstone (1995) as an example, explain interactions in a community.
items.answer: Wolves were reintroduced after 70 years; they reduced elk numbers and changed where elk grazed, allowing willow and aspen to recover along rivers. Changing one population affected many others – birds, beavers and even riverbanks.
items.markingKey: Context (Wolves were reintroduced after 70 years; they reduced elk numbers and changed where elk grazed, allowing willow and aspen to recover along rivers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Changing one population affected many others – birds, beavers and even riverbanks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interactions in a community.

items.stem: A survey finds that the population of a butterfly in a meadow fell by 60% over 10 years. Suggest three biotic and abiotic factors that could explain this, and describe how a scientist could test one of them.
items.answer: Abiotic: warmer/drier summers, pesticide use, loss of habitat (ploughing). Biotic: fewer food plants (nettles, flowers), new predator or parasite, disease, competition. Test: e.g. compare butterfly counts in meadows with and without pesticide use over several years, using transects with the same route, time and weather conditions.
items.markingKey: Abiotic: warmer/drier summers, pesticide use, loss of habitat (ploughing). Biotic: fewer food plants (nettles, flowers), new predator or parasite, disease, competition. Test: e.g. compare butterfly counts in meadows with and without pesticide use over several years, using transects with the same route, time and weather conditions.

items.stem: In grass → rabbit → fox, which organism is the secondary consumer?
items.answer: Fox
items.markingKey: Fox. It eats the primary consumer.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a pyramid of numbers can be an unusual shape.
items.answer: It counts individuals regardless of size; one large tree can feed thousands of insects, so the producer bar is narrow.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It counts individuals regardless of size; one large tree can feed thousands of insects, so the producer bar is narrow. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a herbivore and a carnivore.
items.answer: A herbivore (primary consumer) eats plants; a carnivore eats other animals.
items.markingKey: A herbivore (primary consumer) eats plants; a carnivore eats other animals. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Producers contain 25000 kJ of energy. If 12% is transferred to the primary consumers, how much energy do they receive?

Omar used published data to compare the mass of each trophic level in an ocean food chain (three surveys).

Trophic level | Biomass / g/m²: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 4483.0 | 4289.0 | 4294.0
2 | 441.3 | 426.1 | 448.1
3 | 42.5 | 43.4 | 42.1
4 | 4.4 | 4.2 | 4.2
5 | 0.4 | 0.4 | 0.4

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The biomass decreases sharply at each higher trophic level. Only about 10% of energy and biomass is passed to the next level, because much is lost through respiration, movement and waste.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The biomass decreases sharply at each higher trophic level.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Only about 10% of energy and biomass is passed to the next level, because much is lost through respiration, movement and waste.

items.stem: Using DDT in food chains (1950s–60s) as an example, explain bioaccumulation through trophic levels.
items.answer: The insecticide DDT built up in fish and then in birds of prey such as ospreys; it thinned their eggshells and populations crashed until DDT was banned. Rachel Carson’s book Silent Spring (1962) led to bans and the recovery of many bird species.
items.markingKey: Context (The insecticide DDT built up in fish and then in birds of prey such as ospreys; it thinned their eggshells and populations crashed until DDT was banned.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rachel Carson’s book Silent Spring (1962) led to bans and the recovery of many bird species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bioaccumulation through trophic levels.

items.stem: Maya plans an investigation into how the number of aphids on a plant affects the number of ladybirds feeding there. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (number of aphids per plant (counted)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: In a pond food web, algae are eaten by water fleas and snails; water fleas are eaten by small fish; snails and small fish are eaten by perch. Predict and explain what happens to the other populations if a disease kills most of the snails.
items.answer: Perch eat more small fish (less food available) → small fish decrease → water fleas increase (less predation) → algae may decrease (more grazing by fleas) or increase short-term (fewer snails grazing). Perch may decrease due to less food. Effects depend on how much each species relies on the others.
items.markingKey: Perch eat more small fish (less food available) → small fish decrease → water fleas increase (less predation) → algae may decrease (more grazing by fleas) or increase short-term (fewer snails grazing). Perch may decrease due to less food. Effects depend on how much each species relies on the others.

items.stem: Briefly explain why removing a predator from a food web can affect many other species.
items.answer: Its prey may increase and overeat their food, reducing plant populations and other animals that depend on them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Its prey may increase and overeat their food, reducing plant populations and other animals that depend on them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Arrows in a food chain point from the eater to the food." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Arrows show energy flow, so they point from the food to the organism that eats it.
items.markingKey: Arrows show energy flow, so they point from the food to the organism that eats it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of aphids on a plant affects the number of ladybirds feeding there, state the dependent variable and describe how Sana should measure it.
items.answer: number of ladybirds on the plant after 24 hours
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: number of ladybirds on the plant after 24 hours.

items.stem: Grass in a field stores 20000 kJ/m² per year. The rabbits that eat it gain 1600 kJ/m² per year. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from grass to rabbits.
items.markingKey: M1 efficiency = energy transferred ÷ energy available × 100 = 1600 ÷ 20000 × 100; A1 8%.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "chlorophyll"?
options: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy
A container sunk into the ground to catch small crawling animals
The process in which plants use light energy to make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water
An animal that eats producers (a herbivore)
items.answer: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy
items.markingKey: A. "chlorophyll" is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy.

items.stem: A student claims: "Most of a tree’s mass comes from soil." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most of a tree’s mass comes from carbon dioxide from the air, fixed by photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: Most of a tree’s mass comes from carbon dioxide from the air, fixed by photosynthesis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why plants produce oxygen during the day but take in oxygen at night.
items.answer: In daylight photosynthesis is faster than respiration so there is a net release of oxygen; at night only respiration happens, which uses oxygen. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In daylight photosynthesis is faster than respiration so there is a net release of oxygen; at night only respiration happens, which uses oxygen. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sana is investigating how the distance of a lamp affects the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: distance of the lamp from the pondweed (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: distance of the lamp from the pondweed (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Light intensity is proportional to 1/d², where d is the distance from the lamp. Pondweed makes 40 bubbles/min at 10 cm. Assuming light is the only limiting factor, predict the rate at 20 cm.
items.answer: 10 bubbles/min
items.markingKey: M1 doubling distance → light intensity × ¼ ((10/20)² = 0.25); M1 40 × 0.25; A1 10 bubbles/min.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the distance of a lamp affects the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Place a 10 cm piece of pondweed in 0.1% sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a boiling tube; place a lamp 10 cm away behind a water heat shield in a dark room; leave 5 min to adjust; collect gas for 5 min in a gas syringe; repeat at each distance; repeat three times; plot volume against distance.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (keep water away from the lamp and electrical sockets; lamps get hot). Model: Place a 10 cm piece of pondweed in 0.1% sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a boiling tube; place a lamp 10 cm away behind a water heat shield in a dark room; leave 5 min to adjust; collect gas for 5 min in a gas syringe; repeat at each distance; repeat three times; plot volume against distance.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "stomata".
items.answer: Tiny pores, mainly on the underside of a leaf, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: tiny pores, mainly on the underside of a leaf, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between respiration in plants and photosynthesis.
items.answer: Photosynthesis uses light, CO₂ and water to make glucose and oxygen in chloroplasts, only in light; respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy in mitochondria, all the time.
items.markingKey: Photosynthesis uses light, CO₂ and water to make glucose and oxygen in chloroplasts, only in light; respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy in mitochondria, all the time. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Joseph Priestley’s mouse and mint (1771) shows plants produce oxygen.
items.answer: A mouse in a sealed jar died, but a mouse in a sealed jar with a mint plant survived; the plant “restored” the air. It was early evidence that plants produce the gas animals need – later identified as oxygen.
items.markingKey: Context (A mouse in a sealed jar died, but a mouse in a sealed jar with a mint plant survived; the plant “restored” the air.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It was early evidence that plants produce the gas animals need – later identified as oxygen. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to plants produce oxygen.

items.stem: Describe how to show that light is needed for photosynthesis using a destarched plant, a strip of foil and iodine. Explain the expected results.
items.answer: Destarch a plant in the dark for 48 h; cover part of a leaf with a foil strip on both sides; place in light for several hours; remove leaf, dip in boiling water (kills cells), warm in ethanol in a water bath (removes chlorophyll; no flames), rinse; add iodine. Uncovered part turns blue-black (starch made); covered part stays orange-brown – no light, no photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: Destarch a plant in the dark for 48 h; cover part of a leaf with a foil strip on both sides; place in light for several hours; remove leaf, dip in boiling water (kills cells), warm in ethanol in a water bath (removes chlorophyll; no flames), rinse; add iodine. Uncovered part turns blue-black (starch made); covered part stays orange-brown – no light, no photosynthesis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "eutrophication"?
options: The excess growth of algae in water caused by fertilisers, leading to oxygen loss and death of aquatic life
The insoluble carbohydrate that plants make from glucose for storage
All the populations of different species living in a habitat
A feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment
items.answer: The excess growth of algae in water caused by fertilisers, leading to oxygen loss and death of aquatic life
items.markingKey: A. "eutrophication" is the excess growth of algae in water caused by fertilisers, leading to oxygen loss and death of aquatic life.

items.stem: Explain how fertiliser running off farmland can kill fish in a lake.
items.answer: Algae grow rapidly and block light; plants die; bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen through respiration, so fish suffocate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Algae grow rapidly and block light; plants die; bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen through respiration, so fish suffocate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Animals adapt during their lifetime because they need to." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adaptations are inherited features that become common over many generations because individuals with them survive and reproduce better.
items.markingKey: Adaptations are inherited features that become common over many generations because individuals with them survive and reproduce better. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Kenji counted mayfly larvae (which need well-oxygenated water) at points downstream from a farm drain where fertiliser enters a river.

Distance downstream / m | Mayfly larvae per sample: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
50 | 4 | 5 | 5
100 | 7 | 6 | 6
200 | 10 | 11 | 10
400 | 17 | 18 | 18
800 | 32 | 33 | 32

Calculate the mean mayfly larvae per sample when the distance downstream was 100 m.
items.markingKey: M1 (7 + 6 + 6) ÷ 3; A1 6.3 (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the thickness of fur (insulation) affects the cooling of a model animal, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: volume of water.
items.answer: more water holds more energy
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (volume of water) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: more water holds more energy. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the thickness of fur (insulation) affects the cooling of a model animal. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Fill identical conical flasks with 100 cm³ water at 60 °C; wrap with 0–4 layers of cotton wool held with elastic bands; insert a thermometer through a lid; record temperature after 15 min; repeat three times; plot temperature drop against number of layers.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (hot water can scald – fill flasks on a tray and handle carefully). Model: Fill identical conical flasks with 100 cm³ water at 60 °C; wrap with 0–4 layers of cotton wool held with elastic bands; insert a thermometer through a lid; record temperature after 15 min; repeat three times; plot temperature drop against number of layers.

items.stem: Bees and flowering plants are interdependent because…
options: bees get nectar and the plants are pollinated
items.answer: bees get nectar and the plants are pollinated
items.markingKey: C. Both benefit.

items.stem: Distinguish between competition and predation.
items.answer: In competition organisms struggle for the same resource; in predation one organism kills and eats another.
items.markingKey: In competition organisms struggle for the same resource; in predation one organism kills and eats another. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using The great Pacific garbage patch as an example, explain human impact on ecosystems.
items.answer: Ocean currents concentrate floating plastic debris in the North Pacific; seabirds and turtles eat plastic, and microplastics enter food chains. It shows how waste far from its source harms marine animals and has led to campaigns to cut single-use plastic.
items.markingKey: Context (Ocean currents concentrate floating plastic debris in the North Pacific; seabirds and turtles eat plastic, and microplastics enter food chains.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows how waste far from its source harms marine animals and has led to campaigns to cut single-use plastic. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to human impact on ecosystems.

items.stem: "Introducing a predator to control a pest is better than using pesticides." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Biological control can work but needs careful research before release.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: targets one pest, less chemical pollution. Arguments against: the predator may eat native species (e.g. cane toads in Australia); hard to reverse. Supported judgement: Biological control can work but needs careful research before release. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pitfall trap"?
options: An animal that eats producers (a herbivore)
A community of organisms together with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment
A container sunk into the ground to catch small crawling animals
The process in which plants use light energy to make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water
items.answer: A container sunk into the ground to catch small crawling animals
items.markingKey: C. "pitfall trap" is a container sunk into the ground to catch small crawling animals.

items.stem: A student claims: "Counting the number of plants in one quadrat gives the population of the whole field." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: You must take many random quadrats, find the mean, then multiply by the total area ÷ quadrat area.
items.markingKey: You must take many random quadrats, find the mean, then multiply by the total area ÷ quadrat area. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Isabel plans to investigate how the percentage cover of moss changes with distance from a tree trunk. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same tree and direction (north side); quadrat size; the same person estimating cover; time of year
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: the same tree and direction (north side) – shade and moisture differ around the tree; quadrat size – changes the area sampled; the same person estimating cover – judgement differs between people; time of year – moss growth changes with season. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student placed 10 random quadrats, each 0.25 m², in a 50 m × 80 m meadow and counted 10 buttercups in total. Estimate the number of buttercups in the meadow.
items.answer: 16000 buttercups
items.markingKey: M1 mean per quadrat = 10 ÷ 10 = 1; M1 per m² = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4; M1 area = 4000 m²; A1 4 × 4000 = 16000.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Using apps to identify plants and animals makes field surveys as accurate as expert ecologists."
items.answer: Apps are a helpful start, but accuracy improves when experts verify records.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick, free, encourages participation; large amounts of data. Arguments against: misidentification, especially of similar species; experts can confirm with keys and specimens. Supported judgement: Apps are a helpful start, but accuracy improves when experts verify records.

items.stem: Explain why many quadrats should be used rather than just one or two.
items.answer: Organisms are not evenly spread; more samples give a more representative mean and a more reliable population estimate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Organisms are not evenly spread; more samples give a more representative mean and a more reliable population estimate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Aiko ran a belt transect up a beach from the low-tide mark and recorded the number of limpets per quadrat (three transects).

Distance from low-tide mark / m | Limpets per quadrat: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 25 | 26 | 25
4 | 21 | 19 | 19
6 | 15 | 14 | 14
8 | 8 | 9 | 8
10 | 3 | 3 | 3

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The number of limpets decreases further up the beach from the low-tide mark. Higher up the beach, limpets are uncovered by the sea for longer, so they risk drying out and have less time to feed.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The number of limpets decreases further up the beach from the low-tide mark.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Higher up the beach, limpets are uncovered by the sea for longer, so they risk drying out and have less time to feed.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the percentage cover of moss changes with distance from a tree trunk. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wear gloves when handling soil; wash hands; check for slippery or uneven ground. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wear gloves when handling soil; wash hands; check for slippery or uneven ground); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
options: What eats what, from predator to prey
items.answer: The direction of energy transfer
items.markingKey: B. Arrow points to the eater.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "All the populations of different species living in a habitat"?
items.answer: community
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of community.

items.stem: Why does a plant kept in the dark for 48 hours give a negative starch test?
options: It used up its starch and could not make more without light
items.answer: It used up its starch and could not make more without light
items.markingKey: C. Destarching before an experiment.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Animals adapt during their lifetime because they need to." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adaptations are inherited features that become common over many generations because individuals with them survive and reproduce better.
items.markingKey: Adaptations are inherited features that become common over many generations because individuals with them survive and reproduce better. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a belt transect and a line transect.
items.answer: A line transect records organisms touching a line at intervals; a belt transect places quadrats at intervals along the line, giving more data.
items.markingKey: A line transect records organisms touching a line at intervals; a belt transect places quadrats at intervals along the line, giving more data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a food chain and a food web.
items.answer: A food chain shows one feeding pathway; a food web shows many interconnected food chains, which is more realistic because most animals eat more than one food.
items.markingKey: A food chain shows one feeding pathway; a food web shows many interconnected food chains, which is more realistic because most animals eat more than one food. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why light intensity is an important abiotic factor in a woodland.
items.answer: Plants need light for photosynthesis; tall trees shade the ground, so only shade-tolerant plants grow beneath them, which affects the animals that eat them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plants need light for photosynthesis; tall trees shade the ground, so only shade-tolerant plants grow beneath them, which affects the animals that eat them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Plants get their food from the soil." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis; the soil provides water and mineral ions, not food.
items.markingKey: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis; the soil provides water and mineral ions, not food. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why camels can survive in deserts.
items.answer: They store fat in the hump (energy, and heat loss elsewhere), produce little urine and sweat, have wide feet for sand and long eyelashes against sand.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They store fat in the hump (energy, and heat loss elsewhere), produce little urine and sweat, have wide feet for sand and long eyelashes against sand. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation into how the percentage cover of moss changes with distance from a tree trunk, state the dependent variable and describe how Lukas should measure it.
items.answer: percentage cover of moss in a 0.25 m² quadrat with 100 small squares
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: percentage cover of moss in a 0.25 m² quadrat with 100 small squares.

items.stem: Briefly describe DDT in food chains (1950s–60s) and explain what it reveals about bioaccumulation through trophic levels.
items.answer: The insecticide DDT built up in fish and then in birds of prey such as ospreys; it thinned their eggshells and populations crashed until DDT was banned. Rachel Carson’s book Silent Spring (1962) led to bans and the recovery of many bird species.
items.markingKey: Context (The insecticide DDT built up in fish and then in birds of prey such as ospreys; it thinned their eggshells and populations crashed until DDT was banned.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rachel Carson’s book Silent Spring (1962) led to bans and the recovery of many bird species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bioaccumulation through trophic levels.

items.stem:
Mohammed counted the number of woodlice under logs at different distances from a stream (three logs at each distance).

Distance from stream / m | Woodlice per log: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 34 | 36 | 37
3 | 28 | 27 | 28
5 | 19 | 20 | 20
7 | 12 | 12 | 8
9 | 4 | 4 | 4

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean woodlice per log at 7 m, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 8 (trial 3 at 7 m); mean = 12.0
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (8) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 12.0.

items.stem:
Yusuf counted bubbles from pondweed at different light intensities.

Light intensity / arbitrary units | Bubbles per minute: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 18 | 17 | 17
20 | 26 | 26 | 26
30 | 32 | 32 | 33
40 | 38 | 36 | 38
50 | 40 | 40 | 41

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The rate of bubbling increases with light intensity, but increases by less at higher intensities, starting to level off. At low light, light is the limiting factor; at higher intensities another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature starts to limit the rate.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The rate of bubbling increases with light intensity, but increases by less at higher intensities, starting to level off.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At low light, light is the limiting factor; at higher intensities another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature starts to limit the rate.

items.stem:
Priya counted mayfly larvae (which need well-oxygenated water) at points downstream from a farm drain where fertiliser enters a river.

items.answer: 100 m; range = 1; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 100 m; 1 range = max − min = 7 − 6 = 1; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem:
Maya ran a belt transect up a beach from the low-tide mark and recorded the number of limpets per quadrat (three transects).

Calculate the percentage change in the mean limpets per quadrat between 2 m and 10 m.

items.stem:
Felix used published data to compare the mass of each trophic level in an ocean food chain (three surveys).

Trophic level | Biomass / g/m²: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 4455.8 | 4647.6 | 4515.5
2 | 452.6 | 452.2 | 463.5
3 | 45.5 | 43.9 | 44.4
4 | 4.5 | 4.7 | 4.4
5 | 0.4 | 0.4 | 0.5

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The biomass decreases sharply at each higher trophic level. Only about 10% of energy and biomass is passed to the next level, because much is lost through respiration, movement and waste.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The biomass decreases sharply at each higher trophic level.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Only about 10% of energy and biomass is passed to the next level, because much is lost through respiration, movement and waste.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how light intensity affects the number of daisy plants in different parts of a school field. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wash hands after fieldwork; watch out for stinging plants and allergies. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wash hands after fieldwork; watch out for stinging plants and allergies); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Artificial lighting in greenhouses to grow food all year is a good idea."
items.answer: Worthwhile with renewable electricity and high-value crops; otherwise the energy cost can outweigh the benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher yields and local food in winter; less food transport. Arguments against: electricity costs and greenhouse-gas emissions if from fossil fuels; only worthwhile for high-value crops. Supported judgement: Worthwhile with renewable electricity and high-value crops; otherwise the energy cost can outweigh the benefits. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Explain how intensive farming can reduce biodiversity and describe three ways farmers can reduce this impact.
items.answer: Monocultures remove varied habitats; hedgerow removal destroys nesting sites and food; pesticides kill non-target insects; fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication. Reduce: replant hedgerows and field margins with wildflowers; crop rotation and organic or targeted pest control; buffer strips by rivers and careful fertiliser use; leave areas uncultivated.
items.markingKey: Monocultures remove varied habitats; hedgerow removal destroys nesting sites and food; pesticides kill non-target insects; fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication. Reduce: replant hedgerows and field margins with wildflowers; crop rotation and organic or targeted pest control; buffer strips by rivers and careful fertiliser use; leave areas uncultivated.

items.stem: Describe how you would estimate the number of dandelions on a 40 m × 60 m school field, and calculate an estimate if 20 quadrats of 0.25 m² contain 30 dandelions in total.
items.answer: Lay two tapes along edges; use random number generator for coordinates; place 0.25 m² quadrats at 20 random points; count dandelions in each; mean = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 per quadrat = 6 per m²; field area = 2400 m²; estimate = 6 × 2400 = 14 400 dandelions.
items.markingKey: Lay two tapes along edges; use random number generator for coordinates; place 0.25 m² quadrats at 20 random points; count dandelions in each; mean = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 per quadrat = 6 per m²; field area = 2400 m²; estimate = 6 × 2400 = 14 400 dandelions.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "secondary consumer".
items.answer: An animal that eats primary consumers
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an animal that eats primary consumers. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "ecosystem".
items.answer: A community of organisms together with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a community of organisms together with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The insoluble carbohydrate that plants make from glucose for storage"?
items.answer: starch
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of starch.

items.stem: Distinguish between predation and competition.
items.answer: In competition organisms struggle for the same resource; in predation one organism kills and eats another.
items.markingKey: In competition organisms struggle for the same resource; in predation one organism kills and eats another. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Counting the number of plants in one quadrat gives the population of the whole field." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: You must take many random quadrats, find the mean, then multiply by the total area ÷ quadrat area.
items.markingKey: You must take many random quadrats, find the mean, then multiply by the total area ÷ quadrat area. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a carnivore and a herbivore.
items.answer: A herbivore (primary consumer) eats plants; a carnivore eats other animals.
items.markingKey: A herbivore (primary consumer) eats plants; a carnivore eats other animals. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a habitat and an ecosystem.
items.answer: A habitat is where an organism lives; an ecosystem is the whole system of living organisms and their non-living surroundings interacting.
items.markingKey: A habitat is where an organism lives; an ecosystem is the whole system of living organisms and their non-living surroundings interacting. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between glucose and starch.
items.answer: Glucose is the soluble sugar made in photosynthesis and used in respiration; starch is the insoluble storage form that does not affect osmosis.
items.markingKey: Glucose is the soluble sugar made in photosynthesis and used in respiration; starch is the insoluble storage form that does not affect osmosis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Human impact on ecosystems is always harmful." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some actions help biodiversity, such as nature reserves, hedgerows, breeding programmes and reducing pollution.
items.markingKey: Some actions help biodiversity, such as nature reserves, hedgerows, breeding programmes and reducing pollution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student placed 20 random quadrats, each 0.25 m², in a 20 m × 30 m meadow and counted 20 buttercups in total. Estimate the number of buttercups in the meadow.
items.answer: 2400 buttercups
items.markingKey: M1 mean per quadrat = 20 ÷ 20 = 1; M1 per m² = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4; M1 area = 600 m²; A1 4 × 600 = 2400.

items.stem: Producers contain 80000 kJ of energy. If 15% is transferred to the primary consumers, how much energy do they receive?
Briefly describe Wolves return to Yellowstone (1995) and explain what it reveals about interactions in a community.
items.answer: Wolves were reintroduced after 70 years; they reduced elk numbers and changed where elk grazed, allowing willow and aspen to recover along rivers. Changing one population affected many others – birds, beavers and even riverbanks.
items.markingKey: Context (Wolves were reintroduced after 70 years; they reduced elk numbers and changed where elk grazed, allowing willow and aspen to recover along rivers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Changing one population affected many others – birds, beavers and even riverbanks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interactions in a community.

items.stem: Using Jan van Helmont’s willow tree (1640s) as an example, explain evidence about plant growth.
items.answer: He grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for 5 years, adding only water; the tree gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only 57 g. He concluded mass came from water (partly right); later scientists showed most comes from CO₂ in the air.
items.markingKey: Context (He grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for 5 years, adding only water; the tree gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only 57 g.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: He concluded mass came from water (partly right); later scientists showed most comes from CO₂ in the air. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence about plant growth.

items.stem: Amara is investigating how the thickness of fur (insulation) affects the cooling of a model animal. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: number of layers of cotton wool around a flask (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: number of layers of cotton wool around a flask (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Placing quadrats where there are lots of plants gives better results." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: This introduces bias and overestimates the population; quadrats should be placed randomly.
items.markingKey: This introduces bias and overestimates the population; quadrats should be placed randomly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Key hazard(s): keep water away from the lamp and electrical sockets; lamps get hot. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. items.stem: "Palm oil should be banned to protect rainforests." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Certified sustainable palm oil is better than a total ban, which could shift damage elsewhere.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: palm plantations replace rainforest, threatening orangutans; peat burning releases CO₂. Arguments against: palm oil gives more oil per hectare than alternatives, so other crops could need more land; millions of farmers depend on it. Supported judgement: Certified sustainable palm oil is better than a total ban, which could shift damage elsewhere. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the percentage cover of moss changes with distance from a tree trunk. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Lay a tape measure from the trunk outwards; place a quadrat every 1 m; count the squares more than half covered with moss to give % cover; measure light intensity and soil moisture at each point; repeat on two other similar trees; calculate means.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (wear gloves when handling soil; wash hands; check for slippery or uneven ground). Model: Lay a tape measure from the trunk outwards; place a quadrat every 1 m; count the squares more than half covered with moss to give % cover; measure light intensity and soil moisture at each point; repeat on two other similar trees; calculate means.
